extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and published fiction authors (novelists and short-fiction writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on what to look for and negotiate in literary publishing contracts (novels, short fiction, audiobooks, translations, tie-ins). Covers rights, term length, reversion, ROFR, noncompetes, and when to get legal/agent help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract term / duration (life of copyright vs first printing)
rubrics_metrics.description: In America, contracts are usually for life of copyright for novel contracts with big publishers; short fiction commonly grants first printing only. Around the world and for audiobooks, contracts may be for a certain amount of time with renewals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of geographic differences (UK/Germany often use time-limited terms with renewals). Life-of-copyright novel contracts are standard in the US but can be contested; for short fiction insist on limited first-printing use if possible. Audiobook deals may be time-limited and renewable — check those terms specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversion clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversion clause provides that if your publisher doesn’t meet specified conditions (thresholds of sales, payments, or other conditions), the rights will revert back to you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure a clear reversion mechanism is in the contract. Raise reversion sales thresholds to realistic levels (old low thresholds are easy for publishers to satisfy in the ebook era). If reversion language is weak you may have to buy rights back; better reversion terms can prevent that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perpetual irrevocable rights (especially for short fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts should not ask for perpetual, irrevocable rights that prevent you from removing your work if you later want to dissociate from a market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For short fiction, insist on contractual language that allows you to reclaim or pull your story if needed (e.g., market goes on hiatus or republishing decisions change). Don’t sign away the ability to get out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of ancillary rights / specify exactly what rights are sold
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts should limit which rights the publisher is purchasing (e.g., North American English, maybe North American Spanish), rather than broadly grabbing every possible right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate to retain translation, film, and stage rights where possible. Recognize exceptions (some publishers/markets may seek world English or additional rights). Read the contract language carefully to see how broadly rights are defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio rights negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio rights have become significantly valuable; publishers increasingly want audio rights as part of deals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to fight to keep audio rights if you want them — audio can be a very large revenue source (speakers reported audio as a substantial share of income). Understand market value and weigh whether to license audio separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and international rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation rights are usually sold separately in each country; authors should try to retain the right to sell or license translations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong agent will have relationships with foreign-language agents who can sell translation rights. For short fiction, authors often handle translations directly. Retain translation rights to keep opportunities open (even if many foreign deals are small, they can bring income and promotional value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Film and stage rights — don't give away author-created property
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers retaining film or stage rights means they control those adaptations and typically split proceeds with the author; giving them away on author-created property is generally bad for the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid selling film/stage rights to the publisher for author-created works; exceptions exist (agents or publishers sometimes sell pre-publication). If you must, negotiate terms and know that publishers often profit if Hollywood approaches them. Keep these rights when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared worlds, tie-ins, and work-for-hire are different beasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts for shared worlds, tie-ins, and work-for-hire transfer or restrict rights in ways that differ from standard author contracts (you may not be able to sell certain rights independently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the commercial model (e.g., SerialBox or tie-in properties) and that those contracts will have different terms; read carefully and, where possible, negotiate or understand limitations before signing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of First Refusal (ROFR) — narrow the scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A ROFR is common; it gives the publisher the first opportunity to offer on your next work but should be narrowly defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push to limit ROFR to a narrowly defined next work (ideal: next book in the same series or same media). Avoid broad ROFRs that cover any next work, academic pieces, or unrelated projects. ROFR doesn’t force you to accept an offer but gives the publisher first look.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or narrowly define noncompete clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers have inserted noncompete clauses that try to prevent an author from writing ‘competing’ works while the contract is in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike any noncompete clause if possible; if not, define 'competing work' very narrowly. These clauses can be vague and damaging — push back and use agents/SFWA resources to challenge them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sign away series or character rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Clauses that let the publisher own series rights can give them ownership of your characters and prevent you from using them if you leave the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never sign away series/character rights unless it's explicitly work-for-hire or a publisher-initiated series. Insist the author retain intellectual property for author-created series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract binding on successors, assigns, and heirs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include language that makes the contract binding on successors, assigns, and heirs so obligations/rights transfer correctly after acquisitions or the author's death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause protects you if a publisher is bought or reorganized and ensures obligations (payments, rights) remain enforceable. It also clarifies inheritance of rights for heirs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an entertainment lawyer or an agent experienced in literary contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want a lawyer to review the contract, use someone familiar with literary/entertainment contracts rather than a generic contract lawyer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents should understand standard publishing terms; an entertainment lawyer who knows literature is better for litigation risk and nuanced language. SFWA and other groups can help find experienced reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set realistic, enforceable reversion triggers and thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Old reversion thresholds (e.g., sell X copies) may be meaningless in the ebook era, allowing publishers to meet thresholds without meaningful sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate specific, enforceable triggers (sales metrics, active marketing, out-of-print definitions, time limits) rather than tiny copy thresholds. Consider alternative triggers (publisher inactivity for X years) and explicit remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to boilerplate and recurring bad clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers periodically insert standard boilerplate that may include new or revived problematic clauses (e.g., noncompete language) and will reintroduce them after industry pushback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read every contract carefully; use SFWA/model contracts as references. If a clause appears in boilerplate, challenge it early (collective pushback has removed such clauses in the past).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check royalties and advances (standardized areas but still important)
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties and advances are fairly standardized and extensively discussed elsewhere, but still form a major contractual component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the standard royalty rates and advance norms for your market and format (print, ebook, audio). Consult agents/resources for benchmarks even though this episode skipped deep detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain rights and exploit opportunities for foreign/ancillary sales yourself when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If you retain translation and other ancillary rights, you can license them directly (especially common in short fiction) and potentially earn additional income and visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For short fiction, you may get direct offers from foreign markets — retaining rights lets you accept such offers. Consider submitting to foreign-language markets directly where feasible.
